# The provenance file on Suttungr

*The provenance file for Suttungr. Nothing here is unsourced; that is what the file is for.*

## Provenance

**1. The attestation.** **ᛋᚢᛏᛏᚢᚾᚴᚱ**, from the tradition's own record. On record: Snorri Sturluson, Prose Edda: Skáldskaparmál 3-6 (Kvasir's blood and the mead's brewing; Gillingr's death and Suttungr's ransom of the dwarfs; Hnitbjörg and Gunnlöð; Bölverkr, Baugi, and the auger Rati; the eagle chase and the rhymester's share), with the þulur (jǫtna heiti) and the kennings for poetry, Poetic Edda: Hávamál 104-110 (Óðinn's own account: Suttungr's hall, Gunnlöð's golden seat, Rati's mouth, the ring-oath, and Gunnlöð weeping) and 13-14 (the heron of forgetfulness; 'drunk I was at wise Fjalar's'), Cleasby–Vigfusson, An Icelandic-English Dictionary, s.v. suttungr; Zoëga, A Concise Dictionary of Old Icelandic, s.v. suttungr (name of a giant), de Vries, Altnordisches etymologisches Wörterbuch, s.v. Suttungr (the unsettled etymology).

**2. The narrative record.** **How Suttungr Won the Mead** — When the Æsir and the Vanir made peace, they sealed the truce by spitting into a vat, and from the spittle they fashioned a man, Kvasir, wisest of all beings — no question was asked him he could not answer.  He travelled the world teaching wisdom, until the dwarfs Fjalar and Galar killed him in private, drained his blood into two vats and a kettle named Óðrerir, Boðn, and Són, and mixed it with honey: that is the mead of poetry, of which whoever drinks becomes a skald or a sage. **Bölverkr at the Mountain** — Óðinn set out to take the mead, and he did not take it by force.  Disguised as a wanderer who named himself Bölverkr — 'evil-doer', the one honest name in the whole affair — he came upon nine slaves mowing hay for Baugi, Suttungr's brother, sharpened their scythes on a whetstone, and let them kill each other in the quarrel over it.

**3. The physical record.** Suttungr is a wholly textual giant: no runestone invokes him, no votive deposit names him, and no Viking-Age image can be securely identified with his story. His attestation hangs on the manuscript witnesses of the mead myth — the Codex Regius of the Poetic Edda for Hávamál's account, and the Codex Regius of Snorri's Edda with its fellow codices for Skáldskaparmál's continuous narrative. The story's pictorial life begins only in the early modern North: the eighteenth-century Icelandic paper manuscripts of the Edda (SÁM 66 and the Melsteð Edda) illustrate the myth with woodcut-style scenes — Óðinn as an eagle above the Æsir's waiting vats, Suttungr's eagle behind him — proof of the tale's hold on post-medieval readers, not of older iconography. Claims that figures on the Gotland picture stones depict the mead of poetry remain interpretive and are not accepted as secure identifications; the stone record is silent, and the word-hoard of the skalds — the kennings that kept 'Suttungr's mead' current for centuries — is the only true monument.

**4. The current holding.** The temple at [/suttungr/](/suttungr/), classified Tier 2. One decisive feature survives — a single, honest mark — which places the restoration in Tier-2: exact, and exactly labeled.

**5. The documented resonances.** **Defense, Military & Security**, **Agriculture, Food & Harvest**, **Gaming, Fantasy & Entertainment IP** — seats argued and weighted in the [pattern atlas](/patterns/), read through the myths in this temple's [Resonance File](/suttungr/blog/resonance/).

**6. The primary sources.** [Poetic Edda](/texts/poetic-edda/), [Prose Edda](/texts/prose-edda/) — the library this file answers to, open at the [Sacred Texts collection](/texts/).

**7. The continuing record.** Suttungr's afterlife is the afterlife of the mead itself: every retelling of Norse poetry's origin, from the Kearys' Victorian 'Heroes of Asgard' onward, replays the auger-hole, the golden seat, and the two eagles over the wall of Ásgarðr.  The romantics loved Gunnlöð and made Suttungr a brooding proprietor; the skaldic scholars made him something rarer, a mnemonic fixed point — because 'Suttungr's mead' stayed a living kenning, his name travelled inside every stanza that called verse by its owner's title.
